tagline.text: The tallest pointed rock peak of the Zambales coastal range, the "Mountain of Thunder" trek

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Pre-dawn day hike or 2 days 1 night (about 4–6 hours to the summit)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500~3,500 (per person, rough total including transport from Manila, registration and guide / for a day hike or overnight trip)

children.text: Balingkilat means "thunder" in the Aeta language, and at about 1,100 m it is the highest peak of the Zambales coastal range. During the days of the US Subic naval base it was known as Pointed Peak, and a pre-dawn climb rewards you with sunrise and views over the Anawangin and Nagsasa coast. An Aeta guide is mandatory, and this is a hike for experienced walkers.
Mount Balingkilat rises in the mountains northwest of Subic, in Zambales province. At about

, it is described as one of the highest peaks of the Zambales coastal mountains and coves area. The name is said to mean "mountain of thunder" in the language of the Aeta indigenous people, and American servicemen at the old Subic naval base called it Pointed Peak because of its sharply pointed shape. Its pointed silhouette stands out from the surrounding coast as well.
Philippine mountaineering sites rate the standard route from Sitio Cawag at about 5 to 6 on their 9-point difficulty scale. The summit takes roughly
4–6 hours

, and most of the trail is shadeless grass and rocky slopes, so it is physically demanding. With few trees to block the view, the summit looks out over the South China Sea and coves such as Anawangin, Nagsasa, Talesayen and Silanguin. On a clear day you can also see Mount Cinco Picos beyond the ridge to the east.

The mountain is also the first of the six peaks in the Cawag Hexa traverse, which runs through Balingkilat, Bira-Bira, Naulau, Dayungan, Cinco Picos and Redondo in that order. Climbing Balingkilat alone is very different from tackling the whole Hexa, so if this is your first time, start with Balingkilat only. Its closeness to Manila is part of its popularity. You can leave at night, hike before dawn and be back by midday, so it works as a weekend day trip, but that means walking on very little sleep, so pace yourself. If nearby Mount Cinco Picos feels like a slow ridge walk, Balingkilat is closer to a short, steep rock climb. If you have little hiking experience, build up on easier mountains first.

The area is the ancestral land of the Aeta people. You must hike with an Aeta guide from Sitio Cawag, and independent hikes are not allowed. Registration methods and fees change a little from year to year, so check the latest guidance from the Subic tourism office or the Sitio Cawag community hall before you go. This text is a rough summary based on reviews and guides checked around 2026.

blocks.title: Views from the top of the coastal range

children.text: From the summit you can see the South China Sea to the west and the coves of Anawangin, Nagsasa, Talesayen and Silanguin dotted along the coast. Visibility is best on clear early mornings, and clouds often build up in the afternoon.

After Kawayanan the trail becomes an almost vertical rocky slope. You need your hands in places, so a headlamp is essential in the dark, and your guide picks the line.

The ridge down from the summit is narrow, steep on both sides and covered with loose rock. Guides have hikers move one at a time with space between them, so take care not to knock stones down onto the person below.
Each Aeta guide from Sitio Cawag takes up to five hikers. You walk with locals who know the trail, and the fees go back to the community, so your trip supports the area.

blocks.title: Traverse down to Nagsasa and Anawangin

children.text: A traverse follows the ridge from below the summit down to Nagsasa Cove or Anawangin Cove. The Nagsasa route is known to be about
14 km
from Cawag, with another 4–6 hours after the summit.
The expert route linking six peaks in one day starts at Balingkilat. The first peak alone offers great views and a real sense of achievement, so many hikers make this mountain their only goal.

items.title: Pre-dawn day hike
items.subtitle: Round trip from Sitio Cawag to the summit

children.text: Leave Manila at night by bus or joiner van toward Olongapo and Subic. You need to check in at Sitio Cawag between
in the early morning.

There is guidance to register first at the Subic town fire station and other guidance to pick up paperwork at the Subic tourism office. Ask your joiner organizer or the community hall which one applies.
At the Chieftain's Hall in Sitio Cawag you are assigned a guide and get a short safety briefing.
Start walking with your headlamp on. At first you cross several streams and climb grassy slopes.
You reach the water refill point near Kawayanan. After this the steep, rocky section begins.
Reach the summit and watch the sunrise. It is windy, so bring a light jacket.
The way down follows a knife-edge ridge and rocky sections, so move one at a time with space between you.
Return to Sitio Cawag, tidy up and prepare for the trip back to Manila.
Times are examples based on trip reports. Depending on fitness and weather they can differ by 1 to 3 hours, so follow your guide's judgment.
Take a morning bus from Manila to Subic and finish registration. One trip report describes a schedule that starts around
and reaches the campsite by evening.
Pitch your tent at the camp below the summit and have dinner. The campsite near the summit has no shade and is windy.
Climb to the summit in time for sunrise.
Return to Cawag, or descend toward Nagsasa Cove and take a boat out to Pundaquit.
Boats out of Pundaquit after a Nagsasa traverse can stop running early in the afternoon, so check the schedule in advance.
Take a Victory Liner bus toward Olongapo or Subic from Cubao or Pasay. The fare is about
and the trip usually takes
3–4 hours
You can also take a bus to Iba and ask to be dropped at the Subic police station.
If you get off in Olongapo, take a jeepney or tricycle to Subic town.
Bus schedules and fares change, so check before you leave.
Many hikers use a joiner van that leaves Manila in the evening. It costs about
per person, depending on whether registration is included.
Some operators ask for a deposit of about

From the Subic town fire station to Sitio Cawag is about
20 minutes
by vehicle.
A tricycle costs about
per trip. Search for Sitio Cawag Settlement on Google Maps.
From Clark International Airport (CRK), take a bus toward Olongapo and continue to Subic. The trip takes about
1.5–2 hours
; check schedules and fares locally.

From November to February the northeast monsoon makes the air relatively cool and the skies clearer, so it is the most recommended period. One information site lists October to February as the cool season. About 75% of the trail is exposed to the sun, so a pre-dawn start is standard, but the heat of March to May is hard to bear once midday comes.

From June to September it is the rainy season: the grass is green, but the trail turns muddy and streams swell. The knife-edge ridge and rocky sections become slippery and dangerous, so avoid hiking in this period and during typhoons.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Cool and clear, strong wind at the summit
The most recommended period. You need a jacket in the early morning.
Watch for heatstroke and water shortages. Carry extra water and keep to a pre-dawn start.
Avoid hiking. Check for trail closure notices.
Rain is possible, so check the forecast before departure.

items.label: Registration
items.note: Guidance varies: ₱60, or a ₱100 tourism fee plus a ₱100 tribal fee

items.label: Guide fee
items.note: One guide per five hikers, assigned at the community hall; for the six Hexa peaks a ₱3,000 group fee has also been quoted

items.label: Subic to Cawag tricycle
items.note: About 20 minutes from the fire station to the community

items.label: Joiner van
items.note: Check whether registration and the return trip are included

items.label: Nagsasa Cove entrance
items.note: For the traverse. Quoted as a combined entrance and camping fee; 2022 data listed ₱70 entrance and ₱150 overnight. A separate environmental fee of about ₱20 is paid at the Pundaquit pier. Confirm locally

items.label: Water and food
items.note: 3–5 liters of water needed; bring your own food

There is almost no lodging in Sitio Cawag, so most people either arrive before dawn and start right away or camp on the mountain. On the 2-day route you pitch a tent at the camp below the summit. It is safer to prepare camping gear in Manila beforehand. If you spend the night at Nagsasa Cove after the traverse, cottages and tents can reportedly be rented locally, but prices may change.

You have to handle meals yourself on the mountain, so bring simple food, energy bars and instant rice. After the hike you can find restaurants and convenience stores in Subic town or Olongapo, and spending the night before in town gives you some slack for the pre-dawn check-in. Nagsasa Cove has no electricity or mobile signal, so keep that in mind.
An Aeta guide is mandatory. Independent hikes are not allowed.
Bring 3–5 liters of water. Refills are limited to a few spots such as near Kawayanan, and stream water must always be filtered or purified.
A pre-dawn start is normal. Bring a headlamp and a power bank.
The grass easily scratches arms and legs, so bring long sleeves, long pants, arm sleeves, a hat and sunscreen.
It is not recommended for beginners. It is better to climb two or three smaller mountains first.
Mobile signal varies by section and is weak or absent on the ridges. Download an offline map.
The summit is windy and shadeless, so bring a thin windproof jacket.
On the knife-edge ridge going down, keep a gap from the person ahead to avoid rockfall.
Carry out all your trash, and respect the rules and culture of the indigenous community.

The trail has shadeless grassland, an almost vertical rocky slope and a knife-edge ridge with steep drops on both sides, so heatstroke and falls are real risks. Avoid hiking in the rainy season and during typhoons, and follow your guide's instructions.
The registration place and fee system differ between reports. Get a receipt and use an official counter.
When it rains, streams swell and the rocks get slippery. If the forecast is bad, postpone.
It is easy to get lost in tall grass, so never leave the trail without your guide.
Route guidance for the traverse beyond the summit may not be consistent, so always go with a guide.
After the hike, check the time of the last bus to Manila in advance.
A quiet bay reached by following the ridge down from the Balingkilat summit. It is about
14 km
from Cawag and is one end point of the traverse.
A beach where pine trees meet volcanic-ash sand, and another end point of the traverse that continues from Balingkilat.
Small islands reached by boat from Pundaquit, with beaches and a lighthouse.
Subic town and its coast, a good place to rest before or after the hike.
